text:
But that does not matter. Nothing matters now.

And quite like a little trembling song, her voice sounded in the forest.

And the foliage turns even yellower, autumn is drawing on, a few more stars have appeared in the sky, and from now on the moon looks like a shadow of silver dipped in gold. There was no cold, nothing, only a cool stillness and a streaming life in the forest. Every tree stood thinking. The berries were ripe.

Then came the twenty-second of August and the three iron nights.

XXVI
The first iron night.
At nine o’clock the sun goes down. A dim darkness settles over the earth, a couple of stars can be seen; two hours later, a gleam of the moon can be seen. I wander into the forest with my gun and my dog, I kindle a campfire, and the light from my fire shines in among the pine trunks. There is no frost.

The first iron night, I say. And a bewilderingly fierce joy in the time and the place thrills through me strangely....

A toast, you men and beasts and birds, to the solitary night in forests, in forests! A toast to the darkness and God’s murmuring among the trees, to the sweet, simple harmony of the silence against my ears, to green foliage and yellow foliage! A toast to the sound of life I hear, a snuffling muzzle against the grass, a dog sniffing across the ground! A tempestuous toast to the wildcat lying flat on its throat, taking aim and preparing to spring upon a sparrow in the dark, in the dark! A toast to the merciful stillness on earth, to the stars and to the half-moon, yes, to them and to it!

I rise and listen. No one has heard me. I sit down again.

Thanks for the solitary night, for the mountains, for the sighing of the darkness and the sea; it sighs through my heart! Thanks for my life, for my breath, for the grace of being alive tonight; for that I give thanks from my heart! Listen in the east and listen in the west—no, listen! It is the eternal God! This stillness murmuring against my ear is the blood of all nature seething, God interweaving the world and me. I see a gleaming spider’s thread in the light of my campfire, I hear a boat being rowed in the harbor, an aurora glides up across the sky in the north. Oh, by my immortal soul, I also give great thanks that it is I who am sitting here!

Silence. A pine cone falls dully to the ground. A pine cone fell! I think. The moon is high, the fire flickers on the half-burned firebrands and is about to go out. And late in the night I wander home.

The second iron night, the same stillness and the mild weather.
My soul broods. I walk mechanically over to a tree, pull my cap low over my forehead, and lean with my back against this tree, my hands clasped behind my neck. I stare and think; the flame from my campfire dazzles my eyes, and I do not feel it. I stand in this senseless position for a good while, looking at the fire; my legs are the first to give way and grow tired, and quite stiff-legged I sit down. Only now do I reflect upon what I have done. Why stare at the fire for so long?

Aesop raises his head and listens; he hears footsteps; Eva appears among the trees.

I am exceedingly pensive and sorrowful tonight, I say.

And out of compassion she makes no reply.

I love three things, I then say. I love a dream of love I once had. I love you, and I love this patch of earth. And which do you love most?

The dream.

It grows quiet again. Aesop knows Eva and tilts his head to one side and looks at her. I murmur:

I saw a girl on the road today; she was walking arm in arm with her lover. The girl pointed me out with her eyes and could hardly keep from laughing when I passed.

What was she laughing at?

I do not know. I suppose she was laughing at me. Why do you ask about it?

Did you know her?

Yes. I bowed to her.

And did she not know you?

No, she pretended not to know me.... But why are you sitting there cross-questioning me? It is ugly of you. You will not get me to say her name.

Pause.

I murmur again:

What was she laughing at? She is a flighty creature; but what was she laughing at? In the name of Jesus Christ, what have I ever done to her?

Eva replies:

It was ugly of her to laugh at you.

No, it was not ugly of her! I scream. You are not to sit here and censure her; she does nothing ugly; it was right of her to laugh at me. For Satan’s sake, be quiet and leave me alone, do you hear!

And Eva, frightened, leaves me alone. I look at her and at that very moment regret my harsh words; I fall down before her and wring my hands.

Go home, Eva. It is you I love most; how could I love a dream? It was only a joke; it is you I love. But go home now; I shall come to you tomorrow. Remember that I am yours, yes, do not forget it. Good night.

And Eva goes home.

The third iron night, a night of the utmost tension. If only there had been a little frost! Instead of frost, stagnant warmth after the day’s sun; the night was like a lukewarm morass. I kindled my campfire....

Eva, at times there can be a certain pleasure in being dragged by the hair. So perverse can a human mind become. One may be dragged by the hair down valleys and up mountains, and if someone asks what is going on, one may answer in utter rapture: I am being dragged by the hair! And if one is asked: But shall I not help you, free you? then one answers: No. And if one is asked: But can you endure it? then one answers: Yes, I can endure it, for I love the hand that is dragging me.... Do you know, Eva, what it is to hope?

Yes, I think so.

You see, Eva, to hope is something strange, yes, something very peculiar. One may walk along a road one morning and hope to meet upon that road a person one holds dear. And does one meet this person? No. Why not? Because the person is occupied that morning and is somewhere else altogether.... I came to know an old blind Lapp up in the mountains. For fifty-eight years he had seen nothing, and now he was over seventy. It seemed to him that he saw better and better as time went on; there was steady improvement, he thought. If nothing intervened, he would be able to glimpse the sun in a few years. His hair was still black, but his eyes were quite white. When we sat together in his hut and smoked, he told me about everything he had seen before he became blind. He was hardy and healthy, without feeling, indefatigable, and he preserved his hope. When I was about to leave, he followed me out and began pointing in different directions. There is south, he said, and there is north. First you go in that direction, and when you have gone some way down the mountain, you turn in that direction, he said. Quite right! I answered. And then the Lapp laughed contentedly and said: See, I did not know that forty or fifty years ago, so I do see better now than I did then; it is steadily improving. Then he ducked down and crept back into the hut, the eternal hut, his home on earth. And he sat down before the fire again, as before, full of hope that in a few years he would surely be able to glimpse the sun.... Eva, hope is exceedingly remarkable. I, for example, am now going about hoping to forget the person whom I did not meet on the road this morning.
